title: Rotating Frame of Reference and Fictitious Forces
short_intro: A rotating frame of reference is a non-inertial coordinate system that undergoes rotation with respect to an inertial frame. In such a frame, Newton's laws of motion do not hold unless fictitious forces such as centrifugal and Coriolis forces are introduced.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of inertial and non-inertial frames, centrifugal force, qualitative understanding of Coriolis force, and apparent weight modification.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical derivation of transformation of velocity and acceleration between rotating and stationary frames, Coriolis deflection, Foucault's pendulum, and deviation of falling bodies.

concept_notes.heading: Inertial vs. Rotating Non-Inertial Frames
bullets: An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law of motion is valid, meaning bodies remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
A rotating frame rotates with a constant or time-varying angular velocity ω relative to an inertial frame, making it accelerated and hence non-inertial.
Observers in a rotating frame must introduce fictitious or pseudo forces to apply Newton's laws successfully.

concept_notes.heading: Centrifugal Force
bullets: The centrifugal force is an apparent outward radial force experienced by objects in a rotating frame of reference.
Its magnitude is given by F_c = m(ω x (r x ω)) or mω<sup>2</sup>r for perpendicular distance r.
It acts radially outward from the axis of rotation and is responsible for the reduction of effective gravitational acceleration at the Earth's equator.

concept_notes.heading: Coriolis Force
bullets: The Coriolis force is a deflection force experienced by moving objects within a rotating frame of reference.
Its magnitude depends on the velocity of the particle relative to the rotating frame and is given by F_cor = -2m(ω x v'), where v' is the relative velocity.
It acts perpendicular to both the velocity vector of the object and the angular velocity vector of the rotating frame, causing rightward deflection in the Northern Hemisphere.

concept_notes.heading: Euler Force
bullets: The Euler force arises in a rotating frame when the angular velocity of the frame is not constant (i.e., α = dω/dt is non-zero).
Its magnitude is given by F_Euler = -m(α x r), where r is the position vector from the axis of rotation.
It acts in the transverse direction, producing linear acceleration during non-uniform rotation.

derivations.title: Transformation of Time Derivatives of a Vector
derivations.conditions: Relating a vector measured in a stationary inertial frame S to a rotating frame S' sharing the same origin.
steps: Express any arbitrary vector Q in terms of its components along the unit vectors of the rotating frame: Q = Q_x i' + Q_y j' + Q_z k'.
Take the time derivative in the inertial frame S: dQ/dt = (dQ_x/dt)i' + (dQ_y/dt)j' + (dQ_z/dt)k' + Q_x(di'/dt) + Q_y(dj'/dt) + Q_z(dk'/dt).
Recognize that the time derivative of any unit vector rotating with angular velocity ω is given by du/dt = ω x u.
Substitute these derivatives to yield the operator relation: (d/dt)_inertial = (d/dt)_rotating + ω x.

derivations.title: Transformation of Acceleration to a Rotating Frame
derivations.conditions: Differentiating the position vector r in both frames to find total acceleration.
steps: The position vector r in both frames is identical if origins coincide: r_i = r_r = r.
Apply the operator relation to velocity v_i = v_r + ω x r.
Apply the operator relation a second time to velocity to obtain acceleration: a_i = a_r + ω x v_r + ω x (v_r + ω x r).
Collect terms to isolate the rotating frame acceleration a_r: a_r = a_i - 2(ω x v_r) - ω x (ω x r).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Gravity vs. Latitude
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of effective acceleration g' on the y-axis versus latitude λ (0 to 90 degrees) on the x-axis, showing minimum at equator and maximum at poles.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that centrifugal force reduces gravity maximum at the equator where r is perpendicular to ω and zero at the poles.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct conceptual questions in TGT/PGT on variation of g with latitude.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Foucault's Pendulum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A long pendulum swinging in a plane with a circular trajectory of precession marked on the ground underneath.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct physical evidence of the rotation of the Earth due to the action of the Coriolis force precessing the plane of oscillation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual and descriptive questions in PGT physics exams.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Deflection of Wind/Projectile
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A trajectory curve showing an object thrown straight north deflecting towards the east in the Northern Hemisphere.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the sideways push exerted by the Coriolis force on moving air masses or projectiles.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problem formulation for projectile motion in rotating frames.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the centrifugal acceleration of a point on the Earth's equator. Take Earth's radius R = 6400 km and angular velocity ω = 7.3 x 10^-5 rad/s.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for centrifugal acceleration: a_c = ω<sup>2</sup>R.
Substitute the given values: ω = 7.3 x 10^-5 rad/s and R = 6.4 x 10<sup>6</sup> m.

solved_numericals.question: A body is dropped from a height of 100 m at a latitude of 45° in the Northern Hemisphere. Calculate its eastward deflection due to the Coriolis force. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2 and ω = 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s.
solution_steps: Time of fall t is given by t = \sqrt(2h/g) = \sqrt(2 x 100 / 9.8) = \sqrt(20.408) = 4.517 s.
Eastward deflection formula: s = \frac{1}{3} ω g t^3 \cos(λ).
Substitute values: ω = 7.27 x 10^-5, g = 9.8, t = 4.517, λ = 45°, cos(45°) = 0.7071.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 2 kg moves with a velocity of 5 m/s along the x'-axis inside a coordinate frame rotating with a constant angular velocity ω = 2 rad/s along the z-axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the Coriolis force.
solution_steps: Formula for Coriolis force: F_cor = -2 m (ω x v_r).
Given m = 2 kg, v_r = 5 i' m/s, ω = 2 k' rad/s.
Evaluate cross product: ω x v_r = (2 k') x (5 i') = 10 (k' x i') = 10 j' N/m.
Substitute into force equation: F_cor = -2 (2) (10 j') = -40 j' N.
Magnitude is 40 N acting along the negative y'-axis.

assumptions_and_limitations: The angular velocity ω of the rotating frame is often assumed uniform unless Euler force terms are explicitly included.
Derivations assume standard rigid body rotation where internal distances remain invariant.
Relativistic effects are ignored; classical Newtonian mechanics applies.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force is a reaction force to centripetal force according to Newton's third law.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centrifugal force is a fictitious force acting on masses in non-inertial rotating frames, not a true interactive force pair.
common_misconceptions.why: Newton's third law requires forces to arise from interaction between two bodies; centrifugal force depends on the choice of coordinate system.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Coriolis force performs work on a moving body and changes its kinetic energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: Coriolis force is always perpendicular to the velocity of the particle in the rotating frame, so it does zero work.
common_misconceptions.why: Since W = F . v and F_cor is perpendicular to v, the work done is zero and kinetic energy in the rotating frame remains unchanged by it.

quick_revision: Rotating frames require fictitious forces: centrifugal, Coriolis, and Euler.
Centrifugal force points radially outward: F_c = mω<sup>2</sup>r.
Coriolis force depends on velocity: F_cor = -2m(ω x v_r).
Effective gravity is minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles.
Coriolis force deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
